questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.learningObjective: Explain commerce by distinguishing making a product from bringing it to buyers.
questions.prompt: A workshop makes sandals, a van operator takes them to town, and a stall sells them. Identify the production step and explain how the other two steps illustrate commerce.
questions.answer: Making sandals is production. Selling them is trade, and transporting them supports the trade by getting the goods to where buyers can obtain them.
questions.explanation: Commerce includes exchange and activities that help exchange take place.

markingGuide.description: Identifies making the sandals as production.
Identifies the stall sale as trade.
Explains how delivery supports trade.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.learningObjective: Explain how commerce gives a producer access to markets.
questions.prompt: A cooperative can make more woven baskets than its own village can buy. A retailer in another town places regular orders. Explain one benefit for the cooperative and one for customers in the other town.
questions.answer: The cooperative gains access to more buyers, giving it another outlet for its baskets. Customers in the other town can buy baskets without travelling to the village.
questions.explanation: Commercial links connect producers with customers beyond their immediate area.

markingGuide.description: Explains the benefit of market access for the producer.
Explains improved access for customers.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish promotion from customer service in a trade scenario.
questions.prompt: A shop posts a flyer announcing its new school bags. A week later, a worker helps a buyer report a broken zip. Name the activity illustrated by each action and explain its purpose.
questions.answer: The flyer is promotion and informs potential customers about the bags. Helping with the complaint is customer service and supports the buyer after purchase.
questions.explanation: Promotion communicates an offer. Customer service addresses buyers’ needs or problems.

markingGuide.description: Identifies promotion and its purpose.
Identifies customer service and its purpose.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.subtopic: Money as a medium of exchange
questions.learningObjective: Explain how accepted money allows purchases from different sellers.
questions.prompt: Bola sells a handmade bookmark to one pupil and uses the payment to buy a pencil from another. Explain why both transactions can go ahead even if the pencil seller has no use for a bookmark.
questions.answer: The first pupil pays Bola in money, and the pencil seller accepts that money as payment. The pencil seller only needs to accept the money.
questions.explanation: Money separates the sale of the bookmark from the purchase of the pencil.

markingGuide.description: Identifies money as a commonly accepted means of payment.
Explains how separate sales can occur.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.learningObjective: Explain a limitation of barter that money helps to address.
questions.prompt: In a classroom barter game, Sade offers beans for a clay pot. The pot maker wants cloth, and the cloth owner wants beans. Explain why Sade’s first offer fails and describe a possible exchange sequence.
questions.answer: The pot maker wants cloth, so the first offer fails. Sade can trade beans for cloth, then offer the cloth for the pot.
questions.explanation: Direct barter depends on matching wants. A widely accepted medium of exchange can remove the need to find an extra trading partner.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the mismatch between the first two traders’ wants.
Describes the beans-to-cloth and cloth-to-pot sequence.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish physical cash from funds held in an account.
questions.prompt: Kemi buys a ruler with a naira note. Her parent pays for a workbook using a transfer from an account. Compare what changes hands or changes in the records in the two transactions.
questions.answer: The note physically passes to the seller. With a transfer, the payment moves funds between accounts and appears in the account records.
questions.explanation: Both purchases use money. The transfer changes recorded balances, while the cash purchase passes physical currency.

markingGuide.description: Describes the physical movement of the note.
Describes the change in recorded account balances.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.learningObjective: Classify receipts according to how the money was obtained.
questions.prompt: A pupil receives a birthday cash gift, money for returning an unopened item to a shop, and payment for helping at a family stall. Identify which is earned and explain the sources of the other two receipts.
questions.answer: Payment for helping at the stall is earned. The birthday money is a gift, and the returned purchase money is a refund.
questions.explanation: These receipts increase the cash available for different reasons. Only the stall payment in this example is received in exchange for work.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the stall payment as earnings.
Classifies the other receipts as a gift and a refund.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish money used for a good from money used for a service.
questions.prompt: Chidi buys a replacement bicycle bell and pays a mechanic separately to fit it. Which payment is for a good, which is for a service, and what does Chidi receive for each?
questions.answer: The bell purchase pays for a good, the physical bell. The fitting charge pays for the mechanic’s work, a service.
questions.explanation: The payment for the item transfers the item. The fitting fee pays for work performed.

markingGuide.description: Identifies the bell and explains the good received.
Identifies fitting and explains the service received.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.learningObjective: Treat money as a limited resource and explain a spending trade-off.
questions.prompt: A class has ₦2,400. Cardboard for a required display costs ₦1,500, and optional stickers cost ₦1,100. If the class buys the cardboard first, how much remains? Explain the choice it faces.
questions.answer: ₦900 remains. That is ₦200 short of the stickers, so buying the required cardboard means choosing a cheaper decoration or postponing the stickers.
questions.explanation: The same money cannot pay for both purchases. The essential expense takes priority in this budget.

markingGuide.description: Computes the remaining ₦900.
Explains the shortfall and gives a feasible choice.

questions.subject: Business Studies
questions.learningObjective: Demonstrate honest and courteous conduct in a payment.
questions.prompt: At the canteen, a pupil pays ₦1,000 for a ₦650 meal and is handed ₦450 change. Write what the pupil could say and explain what to do with the extra amount.
questions.answer: “Please check my change. I should have received ₦350, but I received ₦450.” Return ₦100 to the cashier after checking.
questions.explanation: The correct change is the amount paid minus the price. Pointing out the error politely lets the cashier correct the transaction.

markingGuide.description: Finds ₦350 as correct change.
Identifies the extra ₦100 and proposes returning it.
Gives a courteous way to raise the error.
